bio.en: Ian McAllister is the author of the classic product-management essay 'What Separates a Top 1% PM from a Top 10% PM,' a 12-year Amazon veteran who built Amazon Smile and grew Alexa internationally, and now leads global product for Uber's vehicles platform.
bio.zh: Ian McAllister 是经典产品经理文章《是什么让前 1% 的 PM 区别于前 10% 的 PM》的作者，在亚马逊任职 12 年、打造了 Amazon Smile 并推动 Alexa 国际化，如今领导 Uber 车辆平台的全球产品。

summary.en: Ian centers his advice on impact—if you wake up trying to maximize impact rather than politics or promotions, that's the guiding light—and breaks down precisely what separates a top 1% PM from everyone else, for both new and senior PMs. He then goes deep on Amazon's 'working backwards' process: how to implement it on your team, and the common ways teams do it wrong. The episode is a must-listen for PMs at any level, with linked templates and guides in the show notes.
summary.zh: Ian 把建议聚焦于“影响力”——如果你每天醒来都想最大化影响力，而非钻营政治或升职，那就是指路明灯，并精准拆解了前 1% 的 PM 究竟有何不同，分别对初级和高级 PM 都适用。接着他深入亚马逊的“逆向工作”（working backwards）流程：如何在团队落地，以及团队常犯的错误。这期节目是任何层级 PM 的必听内容，节目附注中还附上了相关模板与指南链接。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: If you forget about everything else, forget about politics, forget about promotion, or having a bigger org or whatever, if you simply wake up every day trying to have the biggest impact you can, or if you're a leader trying to use your team to have the biggest impact you can in the company, how you do every part of your day, that's a really good guiding light.
turns.zh: 假如你忘却了其他一切——忘却政治、晋升、打造大型组织或其他任何事物——只要你每天醒来时都致力于创造最大影响力，或者作为领导者努力利用团队在公司内发挥最大作用，如何度过每一天的每一刻，这就是一个极好的指引方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ian, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 伊恩，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah. Man, it's awesome. I'm excited just to spend some time talking with you about product and we'll see what happens.
turns.zh: 太棒了。能与您深入探讨产品相关话题，我既兴奋又期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you expect the impact that this post had when you were writing it, when you were just putting this together, the impact that the post had in your career or just the PM industry?
turns.zh: 您写这篇文章时，是否预料到它会对您的职业生涯或整个产品经理行业产生如此深远的影响？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Definitely not. I used to lurk on Quora at the time and then I was just having fun reading things and answering some questions and I used to look for questions in the Goldilocks zone. They weren't too high level of abstract like how do you be a good problem, but they weren't too super specific and this one was kind of right in the middle. And so I'd pluck off a couple of those and I think more as a way to structure my own thoughts, that was what was interesting and fun for me to do that. Not because I thought it'd have any kind of real reach. But obviously it's been cool to see that people reference it pretty often and that's been pretty fun.
turns.zh: 完全没有预料到。当时我在Quora上潜水，看看回答问题，寻找那种难度适中的问题——既不过于抽象，比如如何成为优秀的问题解决者，也不过于具体。这篇文章正好处于中间地带。我会挑选几个问题，更多是作为整理思路的方式，对我来说很有趣。当时并没想它会有广泛影响。但显然，看到人们频繁引用它，感觉很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll link to this in the show notes. If folks that are listening don't know what we're talking about, we'll link to it and you can check it all out. And we're going to be talking about a lot of this stuff in the actual chat, but there's a couple things there that are worth maybe drilling in on a little bit. One is just the impact that writing on the internet can have on someone's career. This one post I imagine had a lot of impact on the trajectory of your career. Is there something you could share there? Is that true?
turns.zh: 我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。如果听众不了解我们在说什么，我们会提供链接，大家可以查看所有内容。我们在实际对话中会深入探讨许多内容，但其中有几点值得深入探讨。首先，互联网写作对个人职业生涯的影响有多大。您写的这篇文章想必对您的职业发展轨迹产生了巨大影响。您能否分享一些见解？这是否属实？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah, it did. And there's another post, I think it was before this one, someone just asked about Amazon's product development process and so I wrote about the working backwards process. Which isn't my process. I just used it and just described it and just kind of caught on a little bit there as well. I think those two, and then I started to write more about people management and product management. And I think the value for me was so awesome just to make connections with people in the industry and it felt like this is, I guess, the 2010 or something like this where a lot of Amazon people I of thought were just so 100% heads down. It was a little bit of a secretive culture, not maybe like Apple, but it was pretty private. But I was interested in the startup community and product in general and so I think I spent a little time trying to engage with folks and I just made so many great connections and relationships from this.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。还有一篇帖子，我记得是在这之前，有人问起亚马逊的产品开发流程，于是我写了关于倒推式工作流程的文章。但那不是我的流程，我只是用过这个方法，并简单描述了一下，结果还挺受欢迎的。这两篇文章之后，再加上我开始写更多关于人员管理和产品管理的内容，对我来说最大的收获就是能与业内人士建立联系。2010年左右，亚马逊的许多人给我的印象都是埋头苦干，公司文化比较封闭，虽然不像苹果那么神秘，但也相当低调。不过我对创业社区和产品设计很感兴趣，所以我花了不少时间与业内人士交流，结交了很多良师益友。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I remember interacting with you and getting to know Joebot and other folks at Airbnb early on even before I joined. But obviously I'd credit this work and those relationships for me ultimately going there and so many great relationships and people I've met because of it. And aside from just the little positive feedback, I mean people tweet at me periodically, be like, "Hey, by the way, just love this post," and whatever. And so it's super gratifying.
turns.zh: 我记得很早之前就和您互动过，还认识了Airbnb的Joebot和其他人。虽然我还没加入Airbnb，但显然这些经历和人脉对我的职业生涯影响深远。除了偶尔收到用户的积极反馈，比如有人在推特上说：“嘿，顺便说一句，我超爱这篇帖子！”之类的，最让我满足的是写作带来的回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned a little bit about your background and we're about to get into that and I want you to share all the things you've done. But the other piece there that I think is interesting that comes up again and again in the power of writing is it often just starts with you trying to collect your thoughts and putting it out there and ends up, wow, so many people find that valuable and it spreads. And so that's just a really simple way of thinking about if you're starting to write online, just summarize something that you've been thinking about that you want to just crystallize in your own head. There's this quote that's probably falsely attributed to Mark Twain and Hemingway often of just like, I don't know what I've thought until I've written it down. And that's super true with these things and so that's a good example of this.
turns.zh: 您稍微提到了自己的背景，接下来我们会深入探讨。但我觉得写作的力量反复被提及的一个关键点是，写作往往始于你试图整理思绪并将其呈现出来，结果却收获了大量读者的认可和传播。这对初涉网络写作的人来说是个简单易行的思路：先把自己想清楚的东西总结出来，再用简洁明了的语言表达出来。马克·吐温和海明威常被错误引用的名言——“直到写下来，我才真正明白自己的想法”——对此再贴切不过了。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I think with any kind of writing, it was probably less structured initially, but I would, partially because I was trying to share something for an external audience, try to just organize it and make it compact and not too wordy or rambling. And I think business writing, I spent a lot of that time doing that at Amazon, is so valuable because you've got to be a clear thinker to be a clear communicator. And so there's two tests in writing well or communicating well. It's both those things. So I found it's pretty valuable in kind of sharpening your ax.
turns.zh: 我认为任何类型的写作最初都比较松散，但出于要向外部读者分享内容的需求，我会努力组织内容，使其既紧凑又不冗长。比如亚马逊时期的商务写作就非常有价值，因为清晰的思维是清晰沟通的基础。写作和沟通都需要通过两项考验：既要准确传达信息，又要保持语言流畅自然。所以我发现这对提升自己的能力很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So these are the two things we're going to focus our chat on is what makes a top 1% product manager and then the Amazon way of working and especially working backwards. So these are all good cues for where we're going. But before we get there, can you just spend just a minute giving us a sense of some of the wonderful things you've done in your career and what you're up to now?
turns.zh: 接下来我们将重点讨论如何成为顶尖的产品经理，以及亚马逊的倒推式工作方法。这些都是我们探讨的核心议题。但在深入之前，您能否先花一分钟分享一下您职业生涯中的精彩经历以及目前的规划呢？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well, I can tell you what I have done. I'll let others decide what's wonderful or not. So after doing finance and economics in school, I made the logical choice and I got a job doing marketing in the beer industry and then the next logical choice, I moved to Tokyo and I bootstrapped my way into software development without knowing Japanese or software development. Did that for a few years, came back to the states working as a developer at a startup and then kind of a midsize company and then moved to Microsoft as a program manager, pretty much a product manager. The same thing there in that role. Learned some good stuff and then made a connection with Amazon and moved there 2006. And that was really the start of when I think about building my product toolbox and leadership toolbox. So few different things I did over 12 years, a few years in retail and conversion.
turns.zh: 嗯，我可以跟你讲讲我做过的事。至于什么才算出色，还是让别人来评判吧。在完成了学校里的金融和经济学课程后，我做了个合乎逻辑的选择——进入啤酒行业从事市场营销工作。接下来，我又顺理成章地搬到了东京，在完全不了解日语和软件开发的情况下白手起家投身软件开发。这样做了几年后，回到美国，在一家初创公司担任开发人员，之后又跳槽到一家中型公司，最后加入微软担任项目经理，差不多就是产品经理的角色。在那个职位上，我也积累了不少经验。2006年，我转战亚马逊，创建了Amazon Smile项目，负责Alexa业务，领导Alexa国际团队，将Alexa和Echo扩展到六个新国家。最后的职位是负责配送体验和运营，主导多个项目。最近我加入优步，担任高级产品与技术总监，负责车辆业务。这意味着要开发帮助车队和租赁公司让车辆接入优步平台、让司机盈利的工具，涵盖可持续技术、电动化等领域，以及为自动驾驶汽车接入平台铺路。这就是我的职业生涯轨迹。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I then moved in traffic and direct traffic loyalty when I created Amazon Smile. The role in Alexa. I led Alexa International, so scaling Alexa and Echo to six more countries. And the last role in delivery experience and operations. So I led a number of different programs there and then recently joined Uber where I'm a senior director of product and tech for vehicles. So that means everything, all the tools that help fleets and rental companies make their vehicles accessible to Uber drivers so they can earn. Sustainability tech and electrification, our vehicle platform, and then creating a path for autonomous vehicles to come onto the platform. And that's it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我突然意识到，你整个职业生涯的核心是自主性和人工智能，对吧？从Alexa到优步，再到你现在正在研发的自动驾驶汽车技术。这是刻意为之，还是机缘巧合？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I just realized this one thread through your career is autonomy and AI a little bit, right? With Alexa and then with Uber, with these autonomous cars stuff you're working on now. Is that something realized or is that an accident?
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得这两者之间确实有联系。显然，两者都是机器学习和人工智能领域。我这么想是因为我经历了多个不同的人生阶段，尤其是在电商领域，这让我能够涉足各个领域。此外，我想我忘了提在Airbnb与Joebot团队合作的经历——当时我们专注于搭建客户支持技术平台。这也是电商平台的一部分，涵盖了各个方面。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well, I mean I guess you could connect those things. Obviously both are machine learning, AI. The way I think about it is that I've done a whole bunch of different lifetimes, especially around eCommerce, and so it allows me to cover the gamut. Plus, I guess I forgot to mention the time at Airbnb working with Joebot and you and Vlad and Dan and Shirley and there was focused on building out the customer support technology platform. So that's another part of the eCommerce platform. Covers the gamut.
turns.zh: 我也忘了提这一点了。很高兴你提到了这点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I forgot to bring that up too. I'm glad you touched on that.
turns.zh: 我不知道自己怎么忽略了这一点。我想我跳过亚马逊相关的部分了。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I don't know how I missed that. I guess I skipped past that with the Amazon stuff.
turns.zh: 那真是段变革性的时光。现在正好可以聊聊Airbnb和相关经历，探讨如何成为1%顶尖产品经理的秘诀。我知道你的帖子标题是《1%产品经理与10%产品经理的区别》，但我觉得这个话题更广泛——如何成为1%顶尖产品经理。我想或许可以先回顾一下你多年来发现的特质，或者说1%顶尖产品经理需要精通的技能。先简单列举一下，之后我们再详细探讨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The most transformative time getting to work together.
turns.zh: 真是段美好的时光。现在正好可以聊聊Airbnb和相关经历，探讨如何成为1%顶尖产品经理的秘诀。我知道你的帖子标题是《1%产品经理与10%产品经理的区别》，但我觉得这个话题更广泛——如何成为1%顶尖产品经理。我想或许可以先回顾一下你多年来发现的特质，或者说1%顶尖产品经理需要精通的技能。先简单列举一下，之后我们再详细探讨。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: That was awesome. That was awesome. I learned a lot from you too during that time.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我也从你身上学到了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a time. This is a good time to chat about, speaking of Airbnb and all that, to chat about what makes a top 1% product manager. So I know your post was really titled what separates a 1% PM from a 10% PM, but it feels like it's even broader, just like how do you become a top 1% product manager. And I thought maybe a good way to start here is maybe just run through the attributes that you've found over the years or here's the things that a top 1% PM needs to get great at. Maybe just run through them and then we'll talk through them in a little more detail.
turns.zh: 真是段美好的时光。现在正好可以聊聊Airbnb和相关经历，探讨如何成为1%顶尖产品经理的秘诀。我知道你的帖子标题是《1%产品经理与10%产品经理的区别》，但我觉得这个话题更广泛——如何成为1%顶尖产品经理。我想或许可以先回顾一下你多年来发现的特质，或者说1%顶尖产品经理需要精通的技能。先简单列举一下，之后我们再详细探讨。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to pull up my post here so I could actually refer to it. Do you want me to go through all of them or just pick out a couple to touch on?
turns.zh: 是啊，我本来打算把我那篇帖子调出来，这样就能直接引用了。你想让我把所有内容都过一遍，还是只挑几条重点讲讲？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's maybe just go through them quickly just to put them out there and then I'll have some follow up questions to dig into a few of them.
turns.zh: 或许我们先快速浏览一遍，把它们提出来吧，然后我再针对其中几条提问深入探讨。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: All right, sounds good. Well, the way I listed it at the time, think big. Always want to hunt for bigger impact. Communicate, I think we'll probably touch on that a little bit. It's super important for PMs as a test of their thinking and their communication. Simplify. How you can do more with less and have more impact. Simplifying is a great way to do that. Prioritize. That's I think the core skill after communication of a PM and there's so many different lenses to view that. Let's see here. Forecasting and measuring. I think that it's really important. What separates product managers from consultants sometimes is you forecast and then you execute and then you measure and validate and that helps you build your instincts. Just obviously the core execution of just shipping and doing what you said you do. Understanding technical trade offs is that you don't have to be a software engineer to be a great PM, but the more you learn about technical trade offs, not just product and customer trade offs, that will help you simplify and get more yield out of your resources.
turns.zh: 好的，听起来不错。当时我列举的那些技能，首先要放大格局。永远要追求更大的影响力。沟通能力，我觉得我们可能稍微聊聊。这对产品经理来说至关重要，是考验他们思维和沟通能力的试金石。简化。如何用更少的资源做更多的事，产生更大的影响力。简化是实现这一目标的绝佳方法。优先级管理。我认为这是产品经理沟通能力之外的核心技能，有很多不同的视角可以探讨。让我看看。预测与衡量。我觉得这非常重要。有时候产品经理和顾问的区别在于：你先预测，再执行，然后衡量验证，这样能帮助你培养直觉。当然，还有最基础的执行能力——把事情做出来、兑现承诺。理解技术权衡。这并不意味着你必须成为软件工程师才能成为优秀的产品经理，但你对技术权衡的理解越多——不只是产品和客户之间的权衡——就能越好地简化流程，充分利用资源。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Understanding good design. If you're working on anything customer focused, that's always going to help you think in the mind of a customer or user. You don't need to design, but the more you understand helps. Writing effective copy. This goes a long way not to get close and not to sub out the copy to somebody else, but to get good at communicating with a couple words to your customers. That's a great skill. Those were the ones that I wrote at the time, I guess 10 years ago, and then I refreshed the post recently in my newsletter. And I added a couple new ones honestly, because as I reflected back, there was a few that I think a lot about these days that I missed the first time around. Earn trust with others. That's so important as a PM, but especially if you're going to grow as a product leader becomes even more important.
turns.zh: 理解优秀的设计。如果你在做以客户为中心的工作，这总能帮助你站在客户或用户的角度思考问题。你不必亲自设计，但多理解这方面知识很有帮助。撰写有效的文案。这很重要，不要依赖别人代写，也不要敷衍了事，而是要学会用简洁的语言与客户沟通。这是一项很棒的技能。这些都是我10年前写下的，最近我在新闻通讯里更新了内容。说实话，我还添加了几条新内容，因为回顾时发现，有些技能是我现在才深刻体会到的。赢得他人的信任。这对产品经理至关重要，尤其是当你想成长为产品领导者时。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I think trust is the currency of a product manager and a product leader, especially if you're going to grow in your career. Digging for data. It's out there and you got to develop the tools to go find it. Not to depend on your analyst or what's in the reports today. So that's a really important skill for anyone in product. And probably the more junior you are, the more important it is as you're really in the weeds there building product. Pushing back effectively. This is an art and a skill, but I think your ability to do this is pretty correlated with your ability to grow and succeed as a leader. Because if you say yes to everything, you're going to go nowhere. Adapting to change. How you react to change will obviously impact one, your mood and your morale, as well as how effectively you can rally yourself, your team. And then driven by impact, not promotion. Ultimately that's what you want to wake up every day thinking about how to have an impact for your business and that will be an indicator on your likelihood of promotion. So do that instead of just focusing on how to get promoted and having that guide your day.
turns.zh: 我认为信任是产品经理和产品领导者的通行货币，尤其是在职业发展中。如果你想成长，信任就显得尤为重要。挖掘数据。数据就在那里，你需要培养工具去挖掘它，而不是依赖分析师或现有报告。这对产品从业者来说是至关重要的技能。对初级从业者而言尤为重要，因为他们正处于产品构建的基层阶段。有效反击。这是一门艺术和技能，但我认为你能否做到这一点，与你能否成长和成功息息相关。如果你事事答应，那你将一事无成。适应变化。你对变化的反应显然会影响你的情绪和士气，以及你能否有效动员团队。最后，以影响力为导向，而非晋升为导向。最终，这才是你每天醒来时应该思考的——如何为业务创造影响力，而这也将成为你晋升的指标。所以要专注于如何创造影响力，而不是一味追逐晋升，让晋升成为你的行动指南。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So it's a long list. There's a lot that a PM needs to be good at, which I think if you're a PM you already know. It's a wild, crazy, impossible job to have everything nailed down. And at the end of this post even mention you've never met a 1% PM that does all these things. And I think that's important. No one's going to be the best at all these things. And so just to drill down a little bit and get a little more focused. Say you're a new product manager. Of these, I forget how many there, maybe 10, 12, what are the top three that you think new PMs should get most good at and focus on?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以这是一份很长的清单。产品经理需要精通很多技能，我想如果你已经是产品经理了，应该对此心知肚明。想要把所有事情都做到完美，实在是个疯狂、不可思议的任务。文章末尾还提到，从未见过能把所有这些技能都掌握得炉火纯青的产品经理。我认为这一点很重要——没人能在所有领域都做到极致。因此，让我们稍作聚焦，深入探讨。假设你是一位新入行的产品经理。在这份清单中（我忘了具体有多少项，可能10到12项），你认为新手产品经理最应该重点掌握并专注的三项核心技能是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Probably communicate, prioritize, and execute. I think those are just the core building blocks. Other ones will be more important as you grow and become more senior, but those ones, no matter where you are in your product career I think are super important. Being a better communicator is something I've been working on my entire product career and I'll be working on until the day I stop. And I remember years ago I was at Microsoft, my first effectively product manager role and my product unit manager, Thomas, came by the office and I think he asked me, "When is this going to ship?" And I was like, "Well, this thing is taking a little bit longer here and this other thing and yada yada." And I gave a bunch of background, but I didn't really answer the question. And I got a little feedback from him like, that's not really the ... Ultimately he's waiting for a date.
turns.zh: 可能包括沟通、优先级管理和执行能力。我认为这些才是基础的核心技能。随着你职位的晋升，其他技能会变得更加重要，但无论你在产品生涯的哪个阶段，以上三项始终至关重要。提升沟通能力是我整个产品生涯始终致力于的目标，甚至退休前都会继续努力。记得多年前我在微软担任首个产品经理时，团队经理托马斯来办公室问我：“这个功能什么时候能上线？”我支支吾吾回答：“这部分进展有点慢，还有其他事情要处理。”虽然我解释了背景，但根本没回答核心问题。托马斯反馈说这不是重点，最终他只想知道具体的上线日期。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And so I just reflected on that and that was, as I remember, my journey to try to be a better communicator over time and I'm still on it. When I went to Amazon, I worked for Kim Rackmiller who was our, I think at the time, SVP for Worldwide Discovery. And I think she was Amazon's first TPM. And she was tough but super smart. And so that was also an early experience to learn from her. And sometimes you get some feedback when you didn't really answer the question. And my first boss, Russell and I organized and started to gather this thing called the Book of Kim. And so we would gather these best practices that we learned from her elsewhere. Avoid weasel words, answer first and then explain, own your problems. And started building this.
turns.zh: 这让我反思自己多年来如何提升沟通能力，现在仍在努力改进。跳槽到亚马逊后，我跟随金·拉克米勒（当时她是全球探索部门的SVP）工作，她是亚马逊首位产品经理（TPM）。她要求严格但极具智慧，从她身上我学到很多。遇到不回答问题的反馈时，要及时反思。我的第一位上司拉塞尔和我整理了一份《金的宝典》，收集她在其他地方分享的最佳实践：避免含糊其辞、先答后解释、主动承担问题责任等。这些习惯至今仍在延续。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And then I extended that over time and added a bunch more and wrote a post called the Operators Manual. I tried to gather all these things together. But it's such an important thing and the stakes get higher as you work with more and more senior people. But if you can get in the habit early of answering a when question with a date, knowing how to use numbers to answer questions and honestly just learning from feedback and grade yourself after you get feedback on a doc or after a meeting or after answering a question in an elevator. And if you try to say, "Gosh, how could I have done that better?," and then try to get better, you can. And you can go far if you just focus on that and all the other 150 skills of a product manager, but if you don't have that, it's unlikely that you're going to really go too far in your product career.
turns.zh: 随着经验积累，我不断补充内容，最终写成《运营手册》。这些技能至关重要，随着合作对象级别提高，要求也水涨船高。但早期养成习惯很重要，比如用明确的日期回应“何时上线”这样的问题，学会用数据支持论点，虚心接受反馈并自我评估。每次在电梯里回答问题后，都能反思“我本可以做得更好”，然后持续改进。只要专注于这些技能，以及产品经理的其他150项能力，就能走得很远。否则，很难在产品生涯中真正有所建树。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: So that was communicate. I guess prioritize as the next one. And so I think this is the number one key tool of a product manager is prioritization. Because so many things come from being good at prioritizing. And it's not just what project do you do next or do you do this project or that project. There's so many different dimensions to prioritization. There's which themes are you going to prioritize in a roadmap and which projects within a theme and how are you going to sequence those projects, how much of a project you're going to build. And also just time management is also a prioritization function. Like what are you going to choose to spend your time on? Which things are you going to really go all out to make great and which things are you going to starve for attention or just not do? Given the same amount of skill intelligence and resources, a product manager with a great innate ability to prioritize is going to generate 5X the impact of someone without that skill.
turns.zh: 好，我想接下来要讲的是沟通。然后我认为优先级管理是产品经理的首要技能。因为很多事情都源于善于优先级管理。这不仅仅是决定下一个要做哪个项目，或者是选择这个还是那个项目。优先级管理还有很多不同的维度。比如在路线图中要优先处理哪些主题，主题下的哪些项目，以及如何排序这些项目。还有要构建的项目规模。另外，时间管理也是优先级管理的一项功能。比如你要选择把时间花在哪里？哪些事情你要全力以赴做到出色？哪些事情你要刻意忽视，或者直接不做？在技能、智力和资源相同的情况下，一个善于优先级管理的产品经理所创造的影响力，要比没有这项技能的人高出五倍。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: My early, if you could call it success at Amazon, I think was completely dependent. It wasn't because I worked smarter or I was smarter, I worked longer hours or I was more technical than other people. I think it was just because I was one, super hungry for impact. And if there was a number or a metric that measured success at the business I was running, I wanted that to go up and to the right. Not to hit a goal, but just to go as far and as fast up to the right as possible. And if anything, it was just working with a team to hone in on the projects that would do that with the greatest leverage and just marshaling all the team's resources. So that was a good start. That was a fit with Amazon in terms of working backwards from a fitness function or a metric.
turns.zh: 我早期在亚马逊取得的所谓成功，我认为完全取决于这一点。不是因为我更聪明、更努力，或者工作时间更长，或者技术能力更强。我认为只是因为我一方面对产生影响力有着极强的渴望。假如有衡量我所负责业务成功的指标或数据，我希望它能朝着正确的方向上升和增长。不是为了达成某个目标，而是尽可能快速、尽可能远地朝着正确的方向前进。如果说有什么秘诀的话，那就是与团队合作，专注于那些能以最大杠杆作用实现这一目标的项目，并调动团队的所有资源。这是一个良好的开端。这与亚马逊从健身功能或指标倒推的工作方式非常契合。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And so did that with the first team I was there and then again later managed the gifting business. And so it just was one skill that I think helped me as well as make up for maybe some deficiencies I'd had. I don't have the biggest brain in the world and I don't have the biggest working memory and I wasn't the most technical, but by trying to really get good at that prioritization, I think that's helped me and it still does.
turns.zh: 我在第一个团队中就是这么做的，后来管理礼品业务时也是如此。因此，我认为这是一项帮助我克服自身不足的技能。我不是世界上最聪明的人，没有最强的记忆力，也不是最具技术能力的人，但通过努力精通优先级管理，我认为这对我帮助很大，并且至今仍在发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I think execute is the third one, which is no surprise that every PM has to execute. And I think assuming you prioritize well then execution means sort of molding what you want to build into a simple compact package that has the highest impact possible. And then also execution's a big function of the team you're working with. So it's your designers and your data science folks, and especially your engineers.
turns.zh: 我认为执行是第三项技能，毫不奇怪，每个产品经理都必须具备执行能力。我认为，如果你能做好优先级管理，那么执行就意味着要把你想构建的东西打造成一个简单紧凑、影响力最大的包裹。同时，执行也与你合作的团队密切相关。这包括设计师、数据科学团队，尤其是工程师。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: So anything to do with how well they're doing their jobs or how well they're resourced or whether they're getting better and better at every sprint, you have some amount of ownership in helping make that happen because that directly impacts your team's ability to execute and ultimately your reputation as well for being able to execute. The drive that goes into execution, product managers are the mode of power behind execution and impact. And if you stall out or you don't do your job, the project's probably going to stall out as well. And so you're the ones, especially with a TPM, if you're lucky enough to have one in the back of the ship, kind of beating the drum and driving everyone forward. But again, lots of people have written a lot of stuff about execution and there's a lot to it, but I think those are probably the three I'd focus on.
turns.zh: 因此，任何与他们工作表现、资源配置、或在每次冲刺中不断进步相关的事务，你都有责任助力实现这些目标，因为这直接影响团队的执行能力，最终也关乎你个人在执行方面的声誉。推动执行的动力，产品经理是执行和影响力的核心驱动力。如果你停滞不前，或未能履行职责，项目很可能也会停滞不前。因此，尤其是对于那些有幸在团队中配备技术项目经理（TPM）的产品经理来说，你需要充当推动者和领航者，激励团队前进。不过，关于执行力的研究文献浩如烟海，这里我只想重点谈谈三个核心要点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And what's interesting about these three is if you look at the rest of the list, think big, understand technical trade offs, understand good design, I think what I would take away from this is those are the things you don't need to focus on that much when you're a new PM. Focus on, as you said, communication, prioritizing, executing. Focus less on these other things because later they'll become more and more important and obviously learn as much as you can, but it's almost bit easier to think about the things you don't need to stress about when you're starting out.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这三个要点中，如果你看看后续列表中的其他内容——比如高瞻远瞩、理解技术权衡、掌握优秀设计——我认为对新手产品经理来说，更需要关注的是沟通、优先级管理和执行力。而其他技能可以逐步培养，待时机成熟再深入学习。在起步阶段，把精力集中在核心能力上反而更轻松。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah, I think that makes sense. If there's a core or think about in year one as a PM, focusing on those things. And you can develop other skills over time. But yeah, I think you're spot on there.
turns.zh: 没错，我完全赞同。作为新手产品经理，第一年重点关注这些核心能力是明智之选。其他技能可以逐步提升。但关键在于，刚入行时要专注于能带来立竿见影效果的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If we were to go back through these three, just maybe as a last question, and you may not have an answer to this, but if you think about communicating, prioritizing, and executing, is there one tactical thing you could suggest that a PM listening to this can do to get better at one of these things? Is there a trick you've learned of, wow, this is one way you could level up communicating, executing, prioritizing or not?
turns.zh: 如果我们再回顾这三个要点，最后一个问题可能你无法直接回答。但就沟通、优先级管理和执行力而言，你能否给听众一些实用建议，帮助他们在这三个方面有所突破？有没有什么技巧能快速提升他们的能力？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: The closest thing to a checklist, the post I mentioned, the Operator's Manual, that was the closest thing to, if you do these things, these specific actions, I think it'll go a long way. Because a lot of them are guided around not doing the easy pitfalls and communication mistakes like rambling. If you're asked a question and you explain and then maybe you get to the answer, if you just think, answer and then explain or sometimes answer and then shut up, that actually is a tactical thing you can do to get better at communicating. And there's some other tips in there as well. So that was my attempt to try to encode, to take some of the ones that we gathered early at Amazon, add some more. The others are ... Yeah. There's no just simple trick unfortunately to prioritize other than ... I mean I think working backwards is a good technique to have impact to guide your prioritization. And that is something where it's not a simple tip, but there's a set of practices and behaviors that you can do that will ultimately lead you to prioritize better.
turns.zh: 最接近清单的资源——我提到的《运营手册》——里面有一些具体的行动指南，比如避免陷入沟通陷阱和误区。比如，当被问到问题时，如果先解释再给出答案，可能不如先回答再解释更高效。这就是提升沟通能力的实用技巧。手册中还有其他建议。这是我尝试将亚马逊早期总结的经验进行系统化，并补充新观点的成果。其他方面……嗯，优先级管理没有简单技巧，但有一套可行的实践方法，最终能帮助你更好地分配资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We'll talk about all that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会深入探讨这些内容。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And then I think communication, the simple tip was just grade yourself after you communicate and try to just take a moment and after a while you'll just do it naturally to think about, "Gosh, how would I have answered that question better?" And so the next time you could try to answer that question better and it's just a continuous improvement process.
turns.zh: 接下来，我认为沟通很重要。一个简单的小技巧就是，在沟通结束后给自己打分，并花点时间反思：“天哪，我本可以更好地回答那个问题。”这样下次你就能尝试更出色的回答，这就是一个持续提升的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or maybe even ask your manager, "Hey, what could I have done better in terms of how I communicated in that last meeting or that last email?"
turns.zh: 或者你甚至可以问你的经理：“嘿，在上次会议或邮件中，我在沟通方面做得不好的地方有哪些？”

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对的。绝对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so then coming at it from the other direction, say you're a senior PM, what are three of these attributes that you would suggest folks focus on to get better and level up in their career?
turns.zh: 好的，那么从另一个角度来看，如果你是一位资深产品经理，你会建议人们关注哪三个特质来提升自己并在职业生涯中更上层楼？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Gosh, it's still communicate, to be honest. I think that's the one at every level of product, just the stakes are higher. I think think big is one for sure. There was a phrase I think Warren Buffett in the Berkshire Hathaway letter used at some point. Was at our scale we got to hunt for bigger elephants. And so I think at any scale as a PM, whatever your idea is or whatever your solution or the problem you're solving, take a minute at the beginning to say, could this be bigger? Could this be a bigger thing and more impactful than the initial idea, even if the initial idea sounds big? So that's a tool and that's often where I'd start when my PMs were sharing an idea is I'd try to expand it to the degree it might be expanded, think about it from that perspective and then maybe you want to still start small, but with a bigger vision in mind.
turns.zh: 天哪，还是沟通。说实话，在产品领域的每个层级，沟通都很重要。我认为大局观肯定是其中之一。我记得巴菲特在伯克希尔哈撒韦公司的信中曾提到过一句话："以我们的规模，我们必须去猎杀更大的'大象'。" 所以，我认为无论处于哪个层级的PM，无论你的想法是什么，或者你要解决的方案或问题是什么，在一开始就花一分钟思考：这能否更宏大？这能否比最初的想法更有影响力？即使最初的想法听起来已经很宏大了？所以这是一个工具，当我的PM们分享想法时，我通常会先试着把它扩展到可能的极限，从这个角度思考，然后也许你还是想从小处着手，但要怀揣着更宏大的愿景。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Earn trust is a huge one and that's kind of why I added it more recently. And it becomes even more important as you get into senior roles because I think it's truly the currency of a product leader or probably any leader in any function. Because if you want to ask for more resources to do something bigger, if your leadership doesn't trust you to use those resources well or do what you said you're going to do, you're probably not going to get them. But if you've built trust that you're a good steward of resources and you make a lot of impact with a given team, that's directly going to correlate with your ability to gain more resources. Trust is just built by repeatedly setting and meeting expectations. And I think that's a good mantra to think about as a FM. Am I meeting the expectations that I set? And not just doing good things, but calling your shots, forecasting, setting a goal, and then hitting it.
turns.zh: 赢得信任非常重要，这也是我最近特别强调的一点。随着你进入更高级的角色，这一点变得更加重要，因为我认为信任是产品领导者——甚至任何职能的领导者的真正货币。如果你想申请更多资源来做更大的事情，但你的领导层不信任你能善用这些资源或完成你承诺的任务，你很可能得不到这些资源。但如果你建立了信任，证明自己是资源的优秀管理者，并与团队一起创造了重大影响，这将直接与你获得更多资源的能力相关。信任是通过反复设定和实现预期而建立的。我认为作为PM，这是一个很好的座右铭：我是否达到了自己设定的期望？不仅要做好事，还要掌控局面，预测未来，设定目标，然后实现它。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And if you do that repeatedly, you're going to be in pretty good shape. And there's so many practices as a product manager or product leader that build trust. You tell the truth without fail. And you launch when you say you'd launch and you launch what you said you'd launch and you own your mistakes. And then the other practices just lose trust. If you lie or if you're evasive, if you don't ship what you said you're going to do, if you ignore your mistakes or you repeat them. And so I think just simply having high standards for yourself and think of trust as that currency, that's going to correlate well as a PM, as a GPM or director of product in any level, that's the thing that you want to build.
turns.zh: 如果你能反复做到这一点，你的状态就会非常好。作为产品经理或产品领导者，有很多建立信任的实践。比如说诚实无欺。说你要在什么时候上线，就在那个时间上线；说要上线什么，就上线你说要上线的；承认自己的错误。相反，其他做法会失去信任。比如撒谎、闪烁其词、无法兑现承诺、忽视或重复错误。所以我认为对自己设定高标准，并把信任视为货币，这对PM、GPM或任何级别的产品总监来说都是非常重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So thinking big, building trust. Was there a third?
turns.zh: 因此，要敢于放眼大局，树立信任。还有第三个要素吗？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I think maybe the last one, which is certainly relevant for a PM but is really true as well, is driven by impact. And if you forget about everything else, forget about politics, forget about promotion or having a bigger org or whatever, if you simply wake up every day trying to have the biggest impact you can, or if you're a leader trying to use your team to have the biggest impact you can in the company, which will influence how you build your roadmap and how you do every part of your day, that's a really good guiding light. And I remember in my first 10 years at Amazon, just naturally not because I thought about it, I was just hungry to have an impact. Take my business, grow it as fast as possible. I wasn't maybe loosely thinking about promotion, but I wasn't thinking about it. I never talked to my manager about it and I wasn't bringing it up. I was just focused on taking my book of business and making it bigger. And then the net result was I was promoted several times and I did grow in my role, but that wasn't what drove me. It was just the impact.
turns.zh:
我认为最后一个要素或许很重要——对产品经理而言无疑如此，但对任何职场人士而言也同样适用——那就是以影响力为驱动。若你忘却其他一切——忘却政治斗争、晋升机会、管理更大团队等种种考量——只要每天醒来时都致力于创造最大程度的影响力，无论你是产品经理还是团队领导，都能以此为指引，规划路线图，执行每项日常任务。这才是真正的明灯指引。
我记得在亚马逊的头十年，我自然而然地将注意力投向影响力——并非刻意为之，而是出于渴望。专注于拓展业务，尽可能快速成长。当时我或许没有刻意考虑晋升，但也绝未忽视这一点。我从未与经理提及晋升事宜，也从不主动提及。我的精力全放在发展业务上。而最终的结果是，我多次获得晋升，职位也随之提升，但这并非我的初衷——影响力本身才是核心驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you say that driving impact is more important for a new PM or senior PM? It feels like impact is the soup within which all PMs swim and that's constantly important, but it's interesting that you mostly put that into the latter part of a career. Do you feel like with new PMs on your team you're less expecting them to think about impact and focus on impact?
turns.zh: 你认为对新晋产品经理和资深产品经理而言，驱动影响力是否同等重要？似乎影响力是所有产品经理的共同根基，始终至关重要，但有趣的是，你似乎更倾向于将其置于职业生涯后半段。对新团队成员，你是否期望他们更关注影响力而非其他？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well, I mean I think for junior PMs, if you're a brand new PM, then yeah, you want to have an impact, but you're really just ... You have a project or a feature to ship or something like that and you're often not necessarily given a lot of latitude to build your own roadmap. But you're asked to ship this. So you want to spec it, you want to execute and do it. But increasingly as you grow, there are opportunities to sense out and try to have a bigger impact maybe and then start to influence prioritization or roadmaps. It's just that the expectations, it goes from being a nice to have as a junior or first time PM to as you get a little more senior, hopefully if things work the way they should work, that's really how you're evaluated. Yes, you want to treat your team well and you want to do a whole bunch of other things, but take two people, one has a massive impact on the business and one who doesn't, then the right way to work should be that first person should be the one that grows and develops and is tasked and with bigger challenges just because if you're impactful at a bigger challenge, that's even more important for the business. So I think that's a good way to think about the flywheel of product leadership.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为对初级产品经理而言，如果你刚入行，那么确实渴望产生影响力，但通常你只能……比如接手某个项目或功能开发，往往没有太多自主规划路线图的空间，只能专注于交付。但随着职业生涯发展，机会逐渐增多，比如尝试探索如何创造更大影响力，进而影响优先级排序或路线图制定。这种期望值的转变，从初级或首次担任产品经理时的“锦上添花”，到资深后（若一切顺利）成为核心评判标准。这确实需要你以影响力为核心，善待团队，完成其他任务，但比较两个人，一个能对业务产生巨大影响，另一个则相形见绌，那么合理的做法应该是前者获得更多成长与挑战，因为在更高挑战中展现影响力对业务更为重要。因此，我认为这正是产品领导力飞轮的核心逻辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like a lot of times you get lucky as a new PM. You work on a project that ends up having a lot of impact that you didn't necessarily drive. You just happen to work on something that, wow, this was a huge deal and that feels like an important thing to optimize for a little in your early career is work on something that's likely to have a lot of impact even if you're not responsible for setting the strategy and prioritizing.
turns.zh: 初级产品经理常有运气成分。比如接手某个项目，最终产生巨大影响力，而这并非你刻意推动的结果。你只是恰好参与了某个项目，哇，成果意义非凡。这或许是职业生涯初期值得优化的重要方向——即便你不负责制定战略和优先级，也要专注于可能产生巨大影响力的工作。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well, I think that's true if you have a choice in where you work in product. If you have a choice to work on something that's part of offense, something that drives the business. And it's true that executives wake up if something drives dollars or customers or offense things and it just maybe shouldn't be this way, but a little less interested in things that maybe less than a risk that just the risk never happens, it comes to pass or a cost center that operates a little more efficiently. So that it's one lens where that might relate to your success. I think also who you work for. And I think most of us don't get to choose that especially early in our career. It either works out in your favor and which is great and that was the case for me, especially at Amazon, some of the leaders I worked with. But sometimes it doesn't. But I think the more that you can suss out who you work for because then the better they are at these skills and prioritizing, one, they're just going to be a better teacher and a better role model to learn from. So I think that's an important thing to think about in any kind of job change.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为如果你在产品部门有选择工作地点的自由，那这种情况确实存在。如果你能参与推动业务发展、带来收益的项目，那确实如此。高管们往往会对能直接创造营收、获取客户或推动业务发展的项目高度关注，而这或许不该如此。但对那些风险较低、可能永远不会发生的项目，或是能更高效运作的成本中心，他们就没那么上心了。所以从这个角度看，这与你的成功息息相关。我还认为选择为谁工作也很重要。尤其是在职业生涯早期，大多数人没法自主选择雇主。有的运气好，有的则不然。但我认为越早了解雇主的风格越好，因为优秀的领导者更善于设定优先级、分配资源，这样他们就能成为更好的导师和榜样，值得你学习。因此，在任何职场变动中，这都是值得深思的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close the loop on this piece for more senior PMs, the skills to focus on, you said, thinking big, building trust and driving impact. I'll put you on the spot. I'll give you two options, two directions to go with this. One is if you want to get better at each of these three things, do you have any one thing someone could do or what does great look like for thinking big or building trust or driving impact? Those are two options.
turns.zh: 最后对更资深的产品经理们说几句，关于需要重点培养的技能，你提到要具备大局观、建立信任和推动影响力。我来考考你。我给你两个方向去思考。第一个，如果你想在这三个方面有所提升，有没有什么具体的做法？或者说，在大局观、建立信任和推动影响力方面，“优秀”具体是什么样子的？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: That was six questions there Lenny. Let me see here what I'm answering. Well, I think the think big one is interesting and one way to think about thinking big, especially as you grow in your career is most people operate within a box. There's a box of there's product management and these are the things that product managers do. And you basically build a roadmap and you prioritize features and you work with eng. And so that might be the typical kind of product scope and tech. Most of my roles were ones where I was kind of a GM but a really product focused GM and so I naturally found myself taking a much wider view of what product is across disciplines. And I was lucky enough that I had engineering teams and marketers and analysts and other folks and so that helped me. But I think as a PM you can still do that, even if those functions don't report to you, is take that really wide view of what success for your product is and not have the blinders on its product or tech.
turns.zh: 莱尼，你提了六个问题。让我看看我该怎么回答。嗯，我觉得大局观这个概念很有意思。尤其是在职业生涯发展过程中，大多数人会局限于某个框架。比如产品管理就是做路线图、排列优先级、与工程师合作。这可能是典型的产品范畴和技术范畴。我之前的角色更多是担任总经理，但更偏向产品型总经理，所以我自然会更广泛地思考跨学科的产品定义。我很幸运能与工程团队、市场团队、分析师等合作，这对我帮助很大。但我认为即使这些职能部门不向你汇报，作为产品经理，你仍然可以采取更广阔的视角，思考产品成功的定义，不受限于产品或技术范畴。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: It's anything. It's anything that influences the success and your customers' success or anything else. And it just means, you don't own marketing or you don't own this other function, but you own it until you find somebody else to own it. And so that's not necessarily thinking big in terms of scale or whatever, but in terms of how you think about your role as a PM and what your ownership responsibility is. And so I think just the more that you ... You don't want to get over your skis as a PM and then you're trying to change your CFO's mind about something necessarily. But the more you grow, that you have to increasingly do that and find the constraints or barriers to your success or your product success and knock them down no matter what they are.
turns.zh: 任何能影响产品成功、客户成功或其他方面的事物。也就是说，你不必亲自负责市场或其他职能部门，但你要负责到找到合适的人来接手为止。这不一定指在规模或其他方面的宏大视野，而是指你如何看待自己作为产品经理的角色，以及你的责任范围。因此，我认为作为产品经理，你不应墨守成规，试图去改变CFO的想法。但随着你成长，你必须越来越多地这样做，找到制约你或产品成功的因素，并想办法突破它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It makes me think about just the advice of think like an owner, think beyond just your one little bubble, think about the broader business outside of the one little product you might be working on. So that's great advice.
turns.zh: 是啊。这让我想到，关键是要像老板一样思考，跳出自己的小圈子，去思考产品之外更广阔的业务领域。比如你可能正在开发的产品，这只是你关注的一个小点，但你需要考虑整个业务生态。这些建议真是太棒了。
