turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we move on to the working backwards piece, which I'm excited to get into, is there anything else you want to share on this thread?
turns.zh: 在我们深入探讨逆向思考环节之前，你是否还有其他想在本讨论中分享的内容？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I might just talk about earn trust because this is one that I didn't put in there initially and I honestly don't think that I recognized the importance of it early on in my career or even in the middle of my career and it's been in the last couple years that I really understood the importance of it. My wife Sarah is a product manager in AWS and so as I've mentored her a little bit in her career and I've seen how this is really a superpower for her, it really made me reflect like, what are the things I could have done better in different roles to earn trust more? And it's not just the basic things like to be honest and tell two different people the same thing versus different things. I think it's trying to really understand, work backwards from that person and what are their goals and what are their organization's goals and honestly spend the time and the energy to try to get to alignment in the same place.
turns.zh: 我可能只想谈谈赢得信任，因为这是我最初没有纳入的内容。说实话，我在职业生涯早期甚至中期都没有意识到它的重要性，直到最近几年才真正理解其重要性。我的妻子Sarah是AWS的产品经理，所以在指导她职业生涯的过程中，我见证了这对她来说是多么强大的能力。这让我反思，在不同角色中，我本可以做些什么来更好地赢得信任？这不仅仅是基本的事情，比如诚实待人，对不同的人说不同的话。我认为关键是真正理解对方，从对方的角度出发，理解他们的目标和组织的目标，并投入时间和精力来达成共识。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And be willing, not just bullheaded, which I might have been earlier in my career, maybe still to many people, but charging forth what do I think's right but taking some more time to try to forge an alliance with someone because if you do that you're ultimately going to be more successful. So that was just one that I was probably slow to recognize the importance of and I'm trying to catch up now.
turns.zh: 还要愿意放下固执己见的态度——我职业生涯早期可能还这样，现在可能对很多人来说依然如此——而是选择坚持自己认为正确的做法，但同时花更多时间努力与他人建立联盟，因为这样做最终会让你更成功。这是我可能较晚才意识到其重要性的一点，而现在我正在努力弥补。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story that comes to mind where you look back and I should have earned trust there or I broke some trust here that you'd be willing to share?
turns.zh: 你能否回想起某个案例，事后看来你本应该赢得信任，或者你曾破坏了信任，并愿意与我们分享？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: When I was working with you and the team at Airbnb, I think this is one where Joebot brought me on to help build out the customer support technology platform maybe more how Amazon would do it. To maintain a high level of quality but to become more efficient as well and to reduce the cost so that Airbnb wouldn't have to scale customer support this to the same degree the business was scaling. And so trying to build a new team and develop and I was pretty heads down doing it the way I thought it should be done and working with the team there in terms of let's get a strong analytics framework. Let's measure all these things and really understand what's going on at the data level and then let's use the same prioritization muscles that had made me successful at Amazon to prioritize things that were best worked backwards.
turns.zh: 当时在Airbnb与你和团队合作时，我认为乔布特（Joebot）邀请我加入团队，帮助搭建客户支持技术平台，这或许可以借鉴亚马逊的做法——既要保持高水平的质量，又要提高效率并降低成本，使Airbnb无需像业务扩张一样大规模扩展客户支持团队。因此，我专注于组建新团队，开发框架，通过强大的分析工具来追踪数据动态，并运用我在亚马逊成功运用的优先级管理方法，倒推关键优先事项。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I think that what I didn't do as much as I should have is obviously really partnering with the customer support leadership team as well. That was something where I think in some ways it felt like we were in alignment and getting on stage together and stuff, but it turned out I maybe hadn't spent as much time and effort on that as I thought to build that true support there such that that leader would rally the organization around it as well and we'd be marching in the same beat. And so that was something that I would reflect. Now, I think the team did amazing things and Shirley really carrying the torch there in the entire team and so accomplished a lot. But that was a learning about ... Going back, I probably would've spent more time and really tried to do even more on that.
turns.zh: 但我觉得自己本可以做得更好，比如与客户支持团队领导层深度合作。虽然我们表面上看似步调一致，一起登台演讲，但实际上我可能没有投入足够的时间和精力来真正凝聚团队支持，让这位领导者能有效统领全局。我们本应步调一致。但这确实值得反思。如今，整个团队在雪莉（Shirley）的带领下表现出色，已经取得了丰硕成果。但这让我深刻意识到……回过头看，我本应该投入更多精力，真正在此方面下更大功夫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks for sharing that. I never knew that story. And it sounds like the takeaway there is maybe don't take for granted the leadership team, the team that'll actually be using the product. Is that a roughly way to think about it?
turns.zh: 感谢分享这些见解。我之前对此并不了解。看来关键在于不要把领导团队、实际使用产品的团队视为理所当然。是这样理解吗？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well I would say that if you have a certain approach you may be believe it's the right one and it may be the right one, but if you don't build the support and the relationships that they're going to help carry that out and execute on that strategy, it may not get executed as well as you think it should be. And so that's an important part of success. It's a risk that you have to mitigate. And trying to earn trust and to do it that way is a way to mitigate that risk that the right product and the right direction and the right strategy, it may not land if you don't have that support that you need. And so that I think was my learning.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果你有某种方法，可能认为它正确无误，但如果你不建立支持团队，不与他们建立合作关系，他们就无法真正执行你的战略，效果可能不如预期。因此，这是成功的关键部分。这是必须规避的风险。通过努力赢得信任来实现这一目标，是降低风险的有效方式。即便产品、方向和策略正确，如果缺乏必要的支持，也可能无法落地。这就是我的经验之谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What better way to learn a lesson than get some wrong and then you never forget it again.
turns.zh: 吸取教训的最佳方式，就是经历失败并从中反思。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: You could call it getting wrong. Just think of something I could have done better. And just that same continuous improvement mindset. It's to everything, every role, every experience, every project, every communication. And if you build that muscle to try to do it better the next time and also just the try to be a little self aware about what could have gone better, then I think it's a really good muscle to build.
turns.zh: 可以称之为犯错。只需思考自己本可以做得更好的地方。保持持续改进的思维模式。这种思维模式适用于每个角色、每段经历、每个项目、每场沟通。如果你能培养这种不断提升的能力，并保持对可优化之处的自省，我认为这是一项非常宝贵的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to the second area of where our chat is going to go, which is Amazon and things you've learned about just the working backwards process. How many years did you say you worked at Amazon total?
turns.zh: 这自然过渡到我们接下来要讨论的第二个领域——亚马逊以及你在倒推策略方面的经验。你在亚马逊工作了多少年？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: 12 years.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 12 years. It feels like everyone that worked at Amazon is 10 years or more. It's these large numbers. So they must be doing something right and I don't know. What do you think that is actually? Why do people stay there so long? It's amazing.
turns.zh: 12年了。感觉在亚马逊工作的人都待了10年甚至更久。数字太大了。所以他们肯定做对了某些事，我也不知道具体是什么。你觉得到底是什么？为什么人们能在那里待那么久？真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: What's interesting about Amazon, and it's changed over time, is that I think pretty quickly whether you're a fit for it or not. And it can be kind of a crucible and a little spartan. And it just clicked with me though because I'm kind of a structured thinker and right brain. And so this idea that hey, I could have this business and then figure out one metric or fitness function that determines success and then my job is to make that number go up and to the right. That kind of fit with me. And then I rewired my brain probably over the first 10 years around this concept and I just felt like I was learning, I was not only working with smart people that were driven, which was true at Microsoft as well, but there was kind of this DNA in the organization and this wiring that I thought was really effective and it just kind of clicked with me.
turns.zh: 亚马逊有趣的地方在于（而且这点随着时间推移有所变化），你很快就能判断自己是否适合那里。它就像一个熔炉，环境有些苛刻。不过它和我很契合，因为我本质上是个结构化思考者和右脑型人才。所以那种理念——嘿，我可以经营这项业务，然后制定一个衡量成功的指标或适配函数，接着我的工作就是让那个数字上升并保持增长——真的很适合我。前10年里，我把自己的思维方式重塑成符合这个理念的。我感觉自己一直在学习，不仅与那些积极进取的聪明人共事（微软时也是如此），而且整个组织的基因和运作模式都非常高效，这和我很合拍。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And so I molded myself to the environment and at every step of the way I felt like I was learning and growing and one of the benefits for me is you get a chance to learn from so many other people in these different settings. You get the chance to read documents that make you learn more so than probably a slide deck. You get a chance to be in weekly business reviews with really smart people and learn from that. Not just learn from your own experience but from everyone else in that room. So I was just a sponge and so much learning happening that I think propelled my career. And so that was why, especially the first 10 years, that it was so fantastic of just growing and feeling yourself build these new muscles and develop these new tools and I loved it. So that was why I stayed so long and obviously Airbnb then, it was the time to try something new, which was a great experience and kind of a test. I was in Seattle and the company was in San Francisco and spending three days on a road each week was a good learning and ultimately a reason to come back and be Seattle based. But then I chose Amazon again because it was still a great place and I thought I could continue to learn.
turns.zh: 所以我不断适应环境，每一步都感觉自己在成长和进步。对我来说，最大的收获之一就是能在不同场景下向众多优秀人士学习。你有机会阅读那些比PPT更能让你成长的文档，还能和极其聪明的人一起参加每周业务回顾，从中获益。这不仅能从自身经验中学习，还能从同室的每个人那里获得启发。我就像一块海绵，不断吸收知识，这推动了我的职业发展。所以尤其是在前10年里，能在那里成长，感觉自己不断锻炼新技能、掌握新工具，真的太棒了。这就是我留下的原因。后来去Airbnb，是时候尝试新事物了，那也是一次很棒的经历和考验。我在西雅图工作，公司在旧金山，每周三天出差，这段经历很有收获，最终让我选择回归西雅图。但最终我还是选择了亚马逊，因为它依然是个绝佳的学习平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I was going to mention they drew you back in. So yeah, that's pretty rare. What did you learn from folks like Jeff Bezos and Jeff Wilke about building product leadership, company building? What's stuck with you working with folks like?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我正想说他们把你拉回了那里。所以这确实很罕见。从杰夫·贝索斯和杰夫·威尔克那里，你学到了哪些关于产品领导力和公司建设的经验？和他们共事最让你受益的是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I would say two very different people but complimented themselves so well. I didn't have hundreds of meetings with Jeff Bezos while I was there, but I did have a chance, especially in the development of Amazon Smile and then early when I started the social team to have some of those meetings where I wrote the doc and it was Jeff and 10 other people reviewing. The process of doing, even before hitting on Amazon Smile, it was really kind of a innovation process I guess you could call it, where we had a goal in mind to increase customers' loyalty to Amazon, their direct traffic loyalty, not in the way Prime did, which is a paid program, but to try to come up with another program or way in which customers might start their shopping on Amazon instead of elsewhere. And so I was running the gifting business. I moved over to the traffic org to try to come up with a new program with no team or anything.
turns.zh: 我得说他们是两个截然不同的人，但却能完美互补。我在亚马逊期间虽然没和杰夫·贝索斯开过上百次会，但确实有过几次机会——尤其是在开发“亚马逊微笑”（Amazon Smile）项目时，以及我刚组建社交团队初期。当时我写好文档后，杰夫和其他十个人会一起审阅。即便在着手开发“亚马逊微笑”之前，我们其实也在进行某种创新尝试。我们的目标是提升客户对亚马逊的忠诚度——特别是直接流量方面的忠诚度——不像Prime会员那种付费项目，而是想探索一种新方案，让客户习惯从亚马逊而非其他平台开启购物流程。当时我负责礼品业务，后来转到流量部门，试图在没有团队支持的情况下开发新项目。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And then I would meet with Jeff Bezos and Wilke and others every couple months and I would profile a couple different options and use the working backwards process and we'd review some facts. And so there was a bunch of learnings throughout that process. One, I found Jeff to be super encouraging. And each time we'd leave one of those meetings, we maybe didn't find the thing in that meeting. We'd talk about it and brainstorm a little bit, but he would always leave and be encouraging and with a quote. One time he was like, "Remember, this process doesn't have to be efficient because the prerequisite for efficiency is knowing where you're going." And then he'd leave the room and whatever. So I found the rhetoric around Jeff or blowing up or whatever, I didn't find any of that and I found him to be super encouraging and he found all these times to help train me in the working backwards process.
turns.zh: 然后，每隔几个月，我就会和杰夫·贝索斯、威尔克等人开会。我会列出几个不同的方案，运用逆向思维法则，并回顾相关数据。在整个过程中，我们收获了诸多启发。其一，我发现杰夫极具激励力。每次会议结束后，即便我们当场未能达成共识，我们也会进行讨论和头脑风暴。但每次结束后，他总会离开时给予鼓励，并留下激励性的名言。比如有一次他说："记住，这个过程不必追求效率，因为效率的前提是明确方向。"说完便离开了会议室。总之，我从未感受到贝索斯有任何夸夸其谈或情绪失控的迹象。他始终以积极的态度激励我，并多次指导我运用逆向思维法则。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: There was a time when I came with a press release for a concept and it didn't have a problem paragraph. I'd skipped that. And he reviewed it and so forth and he was like, "You know what, maybe if you don't have a problem paragraph, there's not really a problem." And so it was kind of a little lesson to me like, "Yeah, maybe that is why I did it. I wasn't really working backwards, I kind of had the solution in mind and so I'd skipped over that part." So that was one just very specific learning about the process from Jeff. So Jeff Wilke, I probably learned more from Wilke just because I had more exposure over my time there. At one point he was my skip level. And I have such tremendous respect for Wilke or Jaw as he was called internally because he was sort of the consummate operator.
turns.zh:
曾有一回，我带着一份概念宣传稿去找他审阅，却发现里面没有“问题段落”，我直接跳过了这一步。他审阅完后对我说：“你知道吗，也许正因为你没有写‘问题段落’，所以根本就不存在什么问题。” 这让我突然意识到，或许我当初之所以跳过这一步，是因为我心里早有解决方案，却没有倒推整个流程。这是杰夫教给我的一个深刻教训。

杰夫·威尔克（Jeff Wilke）无疑是我在亚马逊学到最多的人——毕竟我在那里待的时间更长。他曾是我的直属上司。我对威尔克（Jeff）或公司内部称他为“Jaw”的这位人物充满敬意，因为他堪称运营大师。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: This muscle that I think you learn working at Amazon about being an operator, whether you're ... You're not in operations, but any part of the business that I think came from him. And I think it was due to him that Amazon developed that muscle. And I think it's one way that separates some Amazon PMs from people who haven't worked there in that environment and that continuous improvement mindset. That's so important. And one of the forums that was a great learning was the WBR or Weekly Business Review. Or later called Consumer Business Review. So this was a forum where Jeff would lead the meeting. It would be a series of metrics for different parts of the business. Everywhere from fulfillment to customer support, to traffic to category teams to programs. And I would present on Amazon Smile there. And the way he would run that meeting and enable you to get through a metrics meeting for the entire North American retail business in one hour.
turns.zh: 我认为在亚马逊工作能让你学到的一项技能，就是如何成为一名运营者——即便你不在运营部门，但只要身处该公司的任何业务部门，这项技能都源自于杰夫·威尔克（Jeff Wilke）。正是在他的引领下，亚马逊才形成了这种强大的运营思维模式。这也是亚马逊产品经理与未曾在亚马逊这种环境中工作过的人，以及缺乏持续改进思维模式的人形成差距的关键所在。这点至关重要。其中一个非常重要的学习平台是每周业务回顾（WBR）论坛，后来更名为消费者业务回顾（Consumer Business Review）。在这个论坛上，杰夫会主持会议，汇总来自不同业务部门的系列指标——从订单履行、客户支持、流量分析，到品类团队和项目管理等各个方面。我曾在亚马逊Smile平台上进行汇报。杰夫主持会议的方式，能让你在一小时内完成整个北美零售业务的指标回顾。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And the way he ran that meeting would lead all those leaders to build these muscles because you wanted to be prepared to speak to the variances or trends in your business in a key metric and know your business and know what you were doing based on that thing. And so just this hour a week of probing and asking questions and everyone ... There might be a hundred people in that room prepared to answer questions about your business. And it had this cascading effect that not only was I or the leaders there on the spot having to answer a question and being prepared, but then I would do the same thing with my team, et cetera. And so I was trying to build those muscles in my team such that they could bring their insights and understanding and actions on things in this cascading effect. So that was a mechanism, which is another really big thing at Amazon that led to all these amazing behaviors.
turns.zh: 他主持会议的方式能促使所有高管养成这种能力，因为你需要为关键指标下的业务偏差或趋势做好准备，深入了解业务并据此采取行动。每周一小时的提问与反馈环节，会议室里可能有上百人随时准备回答有关业务的问题。这种层级效应不仅让在场的领导们必须时刻保持准备，也让下属团队随之效仿。我致力于在团队中培养这种能力，让他们能在层级效应中贡献见解、理解现状并采取行动。这正是亚马逊另一个关键机制，造就了那些卓越的运营文化。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I think a lot of those mechanisms came from Jeff Wilke or he created an environment where they would be developed throughout the organization and then propagated. And so that was one thing, just that operational mindset and rigor that being a product leader is not just about building new things, it's about how well you run what you've already built. And if you're really paying attention to the product that you operate, it will give you ideas for things you could do to double down on something that's happening well or to prevent something bad happening. And I think that's been a very key reason for Amazon's scale. Another thing I really respect about Jeff Wilke, and I think Doug Harrington has some of this as well, is the notion of a little bit of tough love. And I think that's important and that neither were assholes, but sometimes, and especially Wilke, you need to get that look kind of like your dad might look over his glasses at you and be like, "Hey."
turns.zh: 我认为许多这样的机制都源自杰夫·威尔克，或者说他创造了一个让这些能力在全公司范围内发展并传播的环境。这只是其中一项——运营思维和严谨性。这意味着产品经理不仅要打造新事物，更要把已有业务运营得尽善尽美。如果你真正关注所运营的产品，就会获得优化现有优势或预防问题恶化的灵感。我认为这正是亚马逊能实现规模扩张的关键原因。杰夫·威尔克还有一点让我深受敬佩，道格·哈灵顿（Doug Harrington）也具备这种特质，那就是适度严厉的爱。我认为这很重要，他们都不是混蛋，但有时——尤其是威尔克——你需要那种像父亲透过眼镜瞪着你、说“嘿”的眼神。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And so I think that was kind of the vibe that you would get. It was professional, it was respectful, but sometimes everyone needs a little kick in the ass and I think that was something, but it almost builds more respect from him and just incredible leaderly behavior, which I really respect and I try to model and I try to do the same because I respected it so much. And then I guess the last attribute of Wilke, which I really saw was teaching. And it wasn't just saying this is the right thing or this is what my decision is in a meeting, but teaching the why and the pattern, the mental model that informs him to think this is the right thing. And so I think he was just great at teaching, taking a moment. It might just take 10 seconds in a meeting to teach.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这就是你能感受到的那种氛围。那种氛围很专业、很尊重人，但有时每个人都需要被激励一下。我觉得这就是他所做的，但这反而赢得了他的更多尊重，以及令人惊叹的领导才能——这正是我非常敬重并努力效仿的。然后我想提到威尔克的最后一个特质，那就是他在教学方面的卓越表现。这不只是在会议上说"这是正确的做法"或"这是我的决定"，而是教会人们其背后的原因、模式和思维模型，让他们明白为什么要这样做。所以我觉得他非常善于教学，善于花时间停顿下来。会议上可能只需要10秒钟就能传授一个知识点。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And that's something that I've forgotten at different parts of my career, especially as you get more experienced and you know the right decision to do and you know what you want, whatever, that may be the right thing, but I think you'll have a lot more lasting effect if you could abstract it to a degree and teach the lesson. Because then that person will hopefully learn the lesson and can apply it to a bunch of future situations and also understand the why more. And it helps them sometimes disagree and commit more so than just being given prescriptive advice.
turns.zh: 这也是我在职业生涯不同阶段曾遗忘的一点，尤其是当你经验越来越丰富，知道该做什么决定，知道自己想要什么时，虽然这可能是正确的选择，但如果你能将其抽象化并传授经验教训，效果会更持久。因为这样一来，对方就能领会其中的道理，并将其应用到未来诸多场景中，同时更深刻理解背后的逻辑。这甚至能帮助他们在某些情况下更愿意接受不同意见而非一味服从指令。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like it must have been an incredible experience learning from these two. Thanks for sharing all that. I want to get to the working backwards stuff. I feel like we've talked about this a lot. We've talked about this on other podcasts with other guests. I feel like people understand the general idea. Yeah, Amazon works backwards. They write a PR. Maybe there's a six pager thing they do. But I feel like there's not a lot of, here's how actually do this thing. And so just to spend a little time on this, when you see teams trying to work backwards and be like, "Let's work backwards. We're going to be like Amazon.", what do you find they do wrong when they're actually trying to implement this idea of working backwards? What's the most common mistake do you find?
turns.zh: 听起来从他们身上学习一定是段不可思议的经历。感谢你分享这些心得。我想谈谈逆向设计这个话题。我觉得我们已经对此讨论过很多次了。在其他播客中也和其他嘉宾探讨过。我感觉大家都明白这个大致思路。是的，亚马逊会逆向设计。他们会写一份PR文档。或许还会做一份六页的文档。但我觉得真正能将其落地的具体方法却不多见。那么回到正题，当团队试图逆向设计并效仿亚马逊时，他们最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well, working backwards is all about the problem and starting there and obsessing about the problem and being guided by it to then go into the solution. So when teams that do it wrong is they don't do that. They don't work backwards. They have something they want to build. These things look similar. These two technologies or whatever. We could combine them and then do this. And if you say we could and it's not grounded in a customer or customer's problem, you're not working backwards. And then you may use "the working backwards process", but you already have the solution. And so you're adding the problem after the solution. You're retrofitting the problem, retrofitting the customer. And so that I think is the number one thing is that they don't get the importance of truly starting with the problem that you're trying to solve and being faithful to that working backwards from the problem.
turns.zh: 逆向设计的核心在于从问题出发，聚焦于问题，并以问题为导向来制定解决方案。所以做得不对的团队并没有做到这一点。他们没有从问题出发，没有真正逆向设计。他们先有了想开发的东西，比如两项技术或其他产品，然后想把它们结合起来。如果你说"我们可以这样做"，但这并非基于客户或用户的问题，那就不是真正的逆向设计。你只是在套用逆向设计的流程，却已经有了现成的解决方案。于是你是在事后才添加问题、事后才考虑客户需求。所以我认为最关键的一点在于，他们没有意识到真正从要解决的问题出发，并忠实于这个问题的重要性——从问题出发进行逆向设计。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: When I first started at Amazon and community, we had this business of automated merchandising using community content, and that was the core thing we were doing is to grow that. But there was this Jeff idea that a team was super excited about. Because I think in some meeting he'd kind of sketched it out or whatever. And so that there was already all this momentum to build this thing that was actually a Jeff project, but I should have known at the time, in hindsight I do, because the name they had for this project was ASIN to ASIN linking. And ASIN was the identifier for a product on Amazon. And so it was kind of this not working backwards idea ultimately of if you could link to products by a subjected attributes and then you could build a feature around it that allowed customers to vote on these things and then it would be kind of ...
turns.zh: 刚加入亚马逊社区团队时，我们主攻利用社区内容进行自动化营销业务，核心任务就是发展这项业务。但杰夫（Jeff Bezos）提出了一个让团队超级兴奋的想法——因为我记得在某次会议上，他曾简单勾勒过这个构想。所以当时整个团队都充满热情，迫不及待地想把这个项目做出来。这其实是杰夫的一个个人项目，但当时我本该有所察觉——回想起来，现在我明白了，因为这个项目的命名是"ASIN到ASIN链接"，而ASIN是亚马逊平台上产品的唯一标识符。整个项目本质上是反向设计的：如果能根据特定属性链接产品，然后构建一个让客户对这些产品进行投票的功能，那就能……

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: So in spirit, it really wasn't working backwards. But the team was all excited and so we eventually wrote the press release and we did it. And it turned out, it wasn't successful. We ended up shutting it down later. And so I learned a lot, this was the first year or two at Amazon, about using the working backwards process but not really working backwards. And so that's literally, if I'm reviewing a working backwards press release or fact, or even talking with someone about a new initiative, my brain is wired now to not be able to process any information until I focus on the problem and the customer. And then once we start talking about that, then I can engage and literally work backwards to say, okay, how do we solve that problem? And what's the most elegant way to solve it? Or if there's three problems, what's number one or two or three? So it's probably a gap in me that I can't process information without working backwards from the problem, but I find it to be helpful when people do that.
turns.zh: 所以从本质上讲，这个设计思路确实是反向设计。但当时团队太过兴奋，最终我们还是写了新闻稿并上线了这个功能。结果发现它并不成功，后来我们不得不关闭这个项目。这段经历让我深刻认识到，在亚马逊工作的头一两年，我虽然尝试了反向设计的流程，但并没有真正理解其核心理念。如今回想起来，当我审阅反向设计的新闻稿或需求文档时，或者与他人讨论新项目时，我的大脑已经形成了这样的思维模式：在专注于问题和客户之前，我无法处理任何信息。一旦我们开始聚焦于这些要素，我就能顺理成章地反向思考：如何解决这个问题？最优的解决方案是什么？如果有三个问题，哪个是最重要的，第二个和第三个又是什么？所以我可能存在一个缺陷——如果不从问题的角度出发，我就无法处理信息，但我发现当别人这样做时，效果非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when people talk about working backwards, the way you're describing it is interesting where it's focused on start with the problem, which I think generally product teams try to do. Their one pagers their PRDs often have, here's the problem we're solving, here's why it's a problem, here's how we think about ... Is that the core of working backwards? I always imagined it was the launch release and the PR thing and maybe the FAQ. Working backwards at Uber and other and Airbnb, do you actually do that for every project yourself at this point?
turns.zh: 你所描述的反向设计概念很有趣，核心在于从要解决的问题出发。我认为大多数产品团队都会这样做。他们的One Pager、PRD通常会写明：我们要解决什么问题？为什么这是个问题？我们如何思考……这是否就是反向设计的核心？我一直以为反向设计的核心是新闻稿、FAQ以及常见问题解答。Uber和Airbnb等公司是否也为每个项目都这样做？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: There's two parts of it. One, there's the concept of working backwards from what you're trying to accomplish. And I still absolutely do that with my teams as well. What are we trying to accomplish for the business or accomplish for a customer and let's start there. And if they have a problem that is interfering with their ability to be profitable for their ability, if it's a business customer or it's a customer trying to accomplish a goal, starting with that problem. That's different from the working backwards mechanism, which is the press release and the FAQ, which was the mechanism that Amazon used to enforce working backwards, which I think is effective. And I've tried to teach that and write some posts about with templates and things like that because it's a great way to start of the press release has a paragraph about the problem. That's what you write.
turns.zh: 反向设计有两个层面。一是从要达成的目标出发进行反向设计。我现在仍在团队中这样做：我们要为业务或客户解决什么问题？从这里入手。如果客户面临阻碍其盈利能力或达成目标的难题，先从这个问题入手。这与反向设计机制不同，后者是新闻稿和FAQ，而亚马逊正是用这种机制来强制执行反向设计。我曾试图将其推广，并写了一些包含模板等内容的文章，因为这是启动新闻稿的绝佳方式——首段就写明问题所在。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And then you write the solution paragraph and then the customer quote. And then the fact which is is there a legitimate plan to succeed? So if you don't have that muscle to work backwards already and your team, it's a great thing to try, but that's not the only mechanism that can do it. And eventually if you do it enough and you build that muscle to work backwards, you can do it in any number of formats, whether it's something in a PRD or some other way. But the key is that you don't think what we could build, you think about the problem and then the solution that solves that problem.
turns.zh: 接下来，你要写解决方案段落，然后是客户引述。然后是这样一个问题：是否有合理的成功计划？所以如果你团队还没有倒推的能力，那这确实是个值得尝试的好方法，但这并非唯一可行的机制。只要你足够勤加练习，逐渐培养出倒推的能力，你就能以多种形式应用这一方法，无论是产品需求文档（PRD）还是其他形式。但关键在于，你不应只考虑我们能构建什么，而应首先思考所要解决的问题及其对应的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. So the press release is not core to it. It's like a trick to get you to think about the problem you're solving. It's not how you plant announce it.
turns.zh: 明白了。好的。所以新闻稿并非核心。它只是一个让你思考所解决问题的技巧。关键不在于如何正式宣布，而是如何让大家意识到这个问题。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I never thought about it that way. So when you're doing this process at other places outside Amazon, say you're a product leader that's trying to ... I want to improve the way we think about product. What is it that you suggest they do specifically? Is it write out, here's the problem we're solving? Is there more to it? What would you suggest there?
turns.zh: 有意思。我从未这样想过。所以当你在亚马逊以外的其他公司执行这个流程时，比如说你是一位产品负责人，正试图改进我们的产品思维方式。你具体建议他们怎么做？是写出“我们正在解决这个问题”吗？还是有更深层的含义？你能给出什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: If it's a blank slate, truly, you could certainly use the working backwards process like Amazon does with the internal press release and then the fact and so forth. So that's fine. But a lot of companies have a different way they go about it. Some companies are very much, it's slide culture and presentations and so forth. And so as a product leader you could think about what you do with your team and what you do upwards or across. And so you may have the latitude to use any process with your team. And I've done that at some companies where using documents and if they're supportive of the team and they recognize the value of that, like, oh actually this is good and this is a great way to write things down on paper and to have better information content and richer discussion that oftentimes I think people will find that versus a slide with a couple bullets is not great. Then you can build that muscle.
turns.zh: 如果一切从零开始，那确实可以像亚马逊那样使用倒推流程，比如内部新闻稿、事实陈述等。但很多公司有不同的做法。有些公司更倾向于幻灯片文化和演示文稿等方式。作为产品负责人，可以思考如何与团队合作，向上汇报或横向沟通。因此，你可能有自由度在团队中采用任何流程。我曾在一些公司这样做过，如果团队支持并认可其价值，比如“哦，实际上这很棒”——这是在纸上记录信息的好方法，能获得更丰富的讨论内容，往往比只有几个要点的幻灯片效果要好。然后你就能逐渐培养这种能力。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I've found it's a great way to teach and use those to dive deeper into product. But depending on the organization you're at, that may not wash to train your senior leadership to use the process you want to use. And so then it might be a matter of finding the opportunities to try something and saying, "Are you open to doing something this way?" A review of a doc instead of a review of a whatever. So that's a little separate than just working backwards, but I think you just have to acknowledge the environment you're in. And also, unless the organization has a specific format to do this. If it does, you probably just need to use it. Different leaders process information, different ways. You may find one format's effective with your leader, but another one to educate a broader organization. But it's very company specific. So despite what I might want to do, I've just got to recognize that I have more leverage down with my team versus up or across.
turns.zh: 我发现这也是教导和深入探索产品的好方法。但取决于所在的组织环境，这可能不适用于培训高层领导使用你希望他们采用的流程。所以可能需要寻找机会尝试某种方法，然后问：“你们是否愿意以这种方式做事？”用文档审查而非其他形式的评审。这些与倒推流程略有不同，但你必须适应所在的环境。除非组织有特定的格式要求。若有，你可能只需遵循即可。不同领导者处理信息的方式不同。你可能会发现某种格式对你的领导有效，而另一种则更适合教育更广泛的组织。但这因公司而异。所以尽管我可能希望采取某种做法，但我必须承认，与向上或横向沟通相比，我在团队层面更有影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a template that you use consistently? Is that something that you've published of how to frame the problem, how to frame all these other elements?
turns.zh: 你们是否有一直使用的模板？有没有公开的关于如何构建问题的模板，或者如何构建其他这些要素的模板？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I have shared posts on, I know for sure LinkedIn and I probably should put it on the newsletter, on my newsletter, that's a working backwards template and some posts about how to do the process or tips on how Amazon does the process. And so I'll make sure to put those up on my newsletter as well. And the template's free. Obviously anyone could just copy it and grab it.
turns.zh: 我肯定在领英上分享过相关内容，或许还应该把它放到我的新闻通讯里。这是一个倒推式模板，还有一些关于如何开展这个流程或亚马逊如何处理该流程的帖子。我一定会把这些内容也放到我的新闻通讯里，而且这个模板是免费的。显然，任何人都可以直接复制并使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We'll link to that in show notes. Definitely send that to me after we wrap this thing. And I was going to ask, does Amazon work backwards on every product they work on/do you suggest working backwards in every feature and product?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。结束后你一定要把那个发给我。我想问一下，亚马逊在开发每个产品时都会倒推流程吗？还是说你建议在每个功能和产品中都采用倒推思维？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I think there's some scale below which it doesn't probably make sense to do this process because there's a little bit of overhead to it. But I think if it's a new product, absolutely. And I'm sure there's some at Amazon that don't use the process, but in general that was the way and often enforced that you need a working backwards review. Ideally that would happen at the outset, but sometimes it would be added later. And yeah, I think it's a great thing whether you use the mechanism. Again, it's a great template to start with and use if you have the flexibility to, but I think it's also possible just to have the spirit and to try to be true to the spirit of working backwards from what you're trying to do for customers and what problem. That's the most important thing. The template is just a mechanism to help ensure that happens.
turns.zh: 我认为在某些规模较小的项目中，采用这个流程可能不太划算，因为这会增加不少额外成本。但如果是新产品，绝对应该这么做。我确定亚马逊有些团队不使用这个流程，但总体而言，他们一直推行倒推式评审。理想情况下，应该在项目启动时就进行评审，但有时也会在后期补上。这确实是个很棒的流程，无论你是否使用这个机制都很重要。再次强调，如果有条件的话，这个模板是个很好的起点。但最重要的是，要秉持倒推思维，从你要为客户解决的问题出发，忠实于这个核心理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. You mentioned a review. What is that? Working backwards review?
turns.zh: 明白了。你提到了评审，具体是什么？倒推式评审？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Well that would just be a meeting with leadership or other folks to review the concept, review the press release, review the FAQ and ask questions. And in some cases that would be the gate to approving it. That was the case with me and Bezos before we went off and built the team and launched Amazon Smile is I would do these reviews about different concepts and that was the one that we green lit. I mean that's often the case. It's also just a great way to educate other people about what you're trying to accomplish. Ground them in the customer problem and solution. And the FAQ is a whole nother concept. It's about the legitimate plan to succeed. One other thing that I use, I got a chance to have lunch with Jeff Bezos. It was probably back in 2008 or something like this. And I asked him, "What's your criteria for investing in something new?"
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是和领导层或其他相关人员开会，评估概念、审阅新闻稿、解答常见问题并提出疑问的过程。在某些情况下，这甚至是项目获批的关键一步。比如我和贝索斯一起开发亚马逊Smile时，每次都会对不同概念进行这样的评审，最终才确定了这个项目。这很常见。同时，这也是让其他人理解你的项目目标的绝佳方式，让他们深入理解客户问题和解决方案。常见问题解答则完全是另一个概念，关乎成功的合理规划。还有一点，我有机会和杰夫·贝索斯共进午餐，大概是在2008年左右。我问他：“你投资新项目的标准是什么？”

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And he said, "Well it's three things. One, is it a big idea? And then second, is it something we should be doing?" So if maybe you have an idea, if you have this new way to extract oil from shale, is it a big idea? Yeah, probably could be a big idea. Is it something Amazon should be doing? Probably not. And the third test, is there a legitimate plan to succeed? And you got to have all three of those things. And I think the FAQ part of the working backwards process is that early stage legitimate test of whether this thing has a plan. Because you could have this internal press release or big idea or big idea for a solution, but the FAQ basically says, okay, I've thought through the internal components or the finances or the key technical hurdles or whatever. And so that's one that's not written about as much, how to do the FAQ, but I think it's another way to build trust that you've been thoughtful enough given the stage of the product to deserve the resources or deserve to move forward with it.
turns.zh: 他说：“嗯，关键有三点：第一，这是一个宏大的构想吗？第二，这件事我们应该去做吗？” 比如说，你可能有个想法，开发出从页岩中提取石油的新技术——这算不算宏大的构想？很可能是。但亚马逊应该做吗？大概不应该。第三个测试是，是否有合理的成功计划？这三点缺一不可。我认为逆向思考流程中的常见问题解答环节，就是对一个想法是否有合理的成功计划进行的早期验证。因为你可能有内部发布稿、宏大的构想或解决方案，但常见问题解答环节实质上是在说，好吧，我已经仔细考虑了内部组件、财务问题、关键技术难题等等。这部分内容鲜少被提及，但我认为这是建立信任的另一种方式——它能证明你已足够审慎，足以胜任产品开发阶段的资源配置或推进工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. I feel like most PMs listening to this are going to be like, "I always start with a problem. I'm always problem focused so I'm working backwards. So I'm good." Other signs of just like, no, you're not. You think you are but you're probably not doing this well. Is there a symptom of you're not actually doing this correctly?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得大多数听众会觉得：“我总是从问题入手，我总是以问题为导向，所以我在逆向思考。”但有些迹象表明，你并没有真正做好这件事。你自以为是，但很可能做得不好。有没有什么症状能表明你做得不对？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: The most common thing that I see that tips me off is when they talk about something, there's different pieces in the pantry and we have these ingredients, we could put them together, we could add these two things together and make a meal out of it. And so it might be a technology, it might be a service, it might be two different things or the building blocks are there and what's enabled if you add these two building blocks together is something. But that's not really working backwards. It may be true that there's some leverage or some benefit from the company having these technologies or assets, but that to me is often the first step that these two things look similar. We combine them and it's all goodness in this new thing.
turns.zh: 我最常发现的危险信号是，当他们谈论某件事时，比如“厨房里有各种食材，我们可以把它们组合起来，做出一顿美餐。” 这可能是指某项技术、某项服务，或是两个不同元素的组合。这些元素可能存在，但把它们拼凑起来并不能创造出新的价值。相反，这可能只是一种杠杆效应或公司拥有这些技术或资产带来的好处。但对我来说，这往往只是表面相似的第一步。我们把它们组合起来，然后声称这是个新事物。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: So if you start talking about those things or the technology, I think that's a likely case that you're not really working backwards as opposed to the opposite is if there's a customer problem that feels compelling even before the solution, yeah, that does feel compelling. And just like with every startup out there, probably a lot of the pitches are there's a big audience and a painful problem and it's the painkiller versus the vitamin thing. And then we have a novel way to solve that. That's kind of working backwards. But more often, especially in a big company, you'll have all these ideas because you have more ingredients in the pantry of ways you could combine them and try to feed it to someone but may not be working backwards.
turns.zh: 所以如果你开始谈论这些技术或技术栈，我认为这很可能是你没有真正在逆向思考的表现。相反，如果在解决方案出现之前就有一个令人信服的客户问题，那才是真正的逆向思考。比如很多初创公司都会宣传“有庞大的用户群体，存在一个痛苦的问题，我们的解决方案是止痛药而非维生素。” 这才是逆向思考。但在大公司里，尤其是在早期阶段，你可能会有很多想法，因为你手头有各种技术栈，可以组合起来试着推销给别人，但这未必是在逆向思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're reaching about an hour chatting and so I want to let you go. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else you want to share on anything we've chatted about?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们聊了大概一个小时了，该结束了。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的关于我们刚才讨论的内容吗？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Let's see. No. I mean I think we covered a bunch of good ground. It's been fun, but nothing particular.
turns.zh: 让我想想。没有了。我觉得我们已经讨论了很多有价值的内容。很开心，但没有特别想补充的了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Well then we've reached our very exciting lightning round. We've got six questions here. They'll be pretty quick and easy. Whatever comes to mind, share and we'll go through them relatively quickly. Sound good?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。那么我们现在要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。这里有六个问题，都会很简短且容易回答。大家想到什么就分享出来，我们会尽快过一遍。怎么样？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: All right. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you've most recommended to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你最近最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I say Getting Real by 37 Signals and it's specifically the chapter on epicenter design. I've shared that many, many times. You can link to it. That's definitely the most thing I've shared. For fun, The Wool Trilogy by Hugh Howey, he's probably my favorite author and a great series. And then for learning, just a recent one that I thought would be super fascinating was Energy and Civilization by Vaclav Smil. So it might not be on the best seller list, but I thought it was interesting.
turns.zh: 我会推荐37 Signals的《Getting Real》，特别是关于“核心设计”的章节。我分享过很多次，大家可以去看看链接。这绝对是我分享最多的。还有趣味性方面的，Hugh Howey的《羊毛三部曲》，他是我最喜欢的作家，整个系列很棒。学习方面的，我最近觉得非常有趣的是Vaclav Smil的《能源与文明》。这本书可能不在畅销书排行榜上，但我觉得很有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's another favorite podcast of yours other than this one possibly?
turns.zh: 除了这个节目，你还有喜欢的播客吗？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I think How I Built This is really interesting just to decompose how interesting businesses and products came about. And then just because of my work, EV News Daily is a daily digest of what's going on in the electric vehicle space. So that's a very good use of my time, five minutes a day to get up to speed.
turns.zh: 我觉得《How I Built This》很吸引人，能解析很多有趣的商业和产品是如何诞生的。然后因为我的工作，《EV News Daily》是电动汽车领域的每日资讯。这五分钟的阅读对我来说很有效，能快速了解行业动态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very niche. I love it. What's a favorite movie or a TV show you've recently seen?
turns.zh: 很小众，但我很喜欢。你最近看过的喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yellowstone. That's definitely my favorite. Can't wait for the next season. Montana's my happy place, although I'm probably the kind of person that they rail about in the show, so it's kind of ironic. And I think the movie was Everything Everywhere All At Once. I love movies that are not predictable and I thought that was just very creative.
turns.zh: 《黄石》。这绝对是我的最爱。迫不及待想看下一季了。蒙大拿州是我的快乐之地，不过我可能就是剧里那些被吐槽的人，所以有点讽刺。还有电影《平行宇宙》。我喜欢不落俗套的电影，觉得这部电影很有创意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm shocked by how many people on Yellowstone die. That show is just murder left and right. I was not expecting that on a ranch oriented show.
turns.zh: 黄石里死了这么多人真让我震惊。这部以牧场为主题的剧真是凶杀案不断。我完全没想到。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: It's a harsh environment.
turns.zh: 那是个严酷的环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Quite harsh, turns out. Especially if you mess with the Duttons. Next question. Favorite interview question that you like to ask.
turns.zh: 结果发现确实很严酷。尤其是如果你招惹杜顿一家的话。下一个问题。你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: When I'm coming out of left field, I ask people at this stage in your career, what have you learned about yourself? How are you different from other people? No one's prepared for that.
turns.zh: 当我抛出一个出乎意料的问题时，我会问处于你这个职业阶段的人，你对自己有了哪些了解？你和其他人有什么不同？没人能准备好回答这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in their answers?
turns.zh: 你怎么看待他们的回答？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I don't know. There's not one specific thing and there's no right answer, which maybe makes it unfair, but just maybe a little self-reflection and maybe they will have understanding their strengths and that might be a good bit of self-awareness about what makes them different, where they can harness that and that makes them a better PM or engineer or something. And so that's kind of what I'm looking for, but there's no set answer. It's more just to throw them off balance.
turns.zh: 我不知道。没有一个特定的标准答案，可能这让问题有点不公平，但我希望能引发他们的反思，也许他们会认识到自己的优势，了解自己与众不同的地方，进而利用这些特质成为更好的产品经理、工程师之类的。所以这就是我希望得到的答案，但没有固定的模板。主要是想让他们措手不及。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Favorite app right now.
turns.zh: 有意思。你现在最喜欢的应用是什么？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: It's probably not too interesting, but to be honest, YouTube. It's like the eighth wander of the world and just every day I'm amazed if I want to learn about something new. A couple summers ago I had some time off and so I basically taught myself how to do woodworking and built a kitchen and other stuff. And so it's just like it continues to be this resource and this jewel that helps me grow and learn about anything.
turns.zh: 可能这听起来不算太有趣，但说实话，我对YouTube的喜爱简直无与伦比。它就像是世界第八大奇迹，每一天只要我想了解新事物，它总能给我惊喜。几年前的夏天，我有段空闲时间，就自学了木工手艺，还建造了厨房等家具。YouTube始终是那个能让我不断成长、学习的资源宝库，简直是个无价之宝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine some people are watching this on YouTube right now.
turns.zh: 我猜现在就有观众正在YouTube上观看这段视频。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just read a story about an Olympic javelin thrower who learned how to do this watching YouTube. He was somewhere in, I think maybe Africa. He had no coaches around and he just watched this one other javelin guy that just shared lessons on how to do this and became incredibly good. It's insane.
turns.zh: 我刚读到一个奥运标枪运动员的故事，他通过YouTube自学了标枪技巧。他当时在非洲某个地方，周围没有教练指导，就通过观看其他标枪运动员的教学视频，练就了高超的技艺。这太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: And I mean, I'm old, so I didn't have this when I was growing up. I remember going to the library and sending away for a brochure in the back of a magazine and things. Learning was not so easy back then. The internet obviously was a huge resource and is, but then YouTube as well to see somebody do it. It's also interesting to see somebody live. So anyway, I'm a fan.
turns.zh: 说真的，我已经老了，小时候可没有这样的资源。我记得那时去图书馆，翻找杂志后页的宣传册获取信息。学习可没这么方便。如今互联网固然是宝贵资源，但YouTube同样重要——能看到别人现场演示的教学视频，效果更是惊人。所以总之，我就是YouTube的忠实粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. Who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader, someone you look up to?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。在业界，你最尊敬的思想领袖是谁，最敬佩的人是谁？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: I say Gibson Biddle. I think that he is one, just tremendous amount of product experience that I think is valuable. I respect the fact that he takes the time to share it. He doesn't have to, but he does. And he's also a great communicator and he invests in being ... You can tell he measures [inaudible 01:03:02] of his talks and things like this. He's invested over his career to be a great communicator. So I think he's a good role model for me and I think for others out there.
turns.zh: 我选Gibson Biddle。他在产品经验方面极其丰富，这种专业知识非常宝贵。他愿意分享知识，完全没必要这样做，却坚持如此。他沟通能力出色，一直致力于成为优秀的沟通者。从他职业生涯中可以看出，他为此付出了很多努力。所以我认为他是我的榜样，也是许多人的榜样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That guy's a force. I'm happy that we've had him on this podcast. I'm hoping that everyone eventually, that people mention in this question we end up having on this podcast. So that's great to check. I also love Gibson. He's got a great newsletter. Askgibbs.substack.com I think. Ian, thank you so much for being here. This was amazing. I really appreciate you sharing all this wisdom with us. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这家伙真是了不起。很高兴能邀请他参加我们的播客。希望未来能有更多嘉宾参与到我们这个节目中来。这太棒了。我也超爱Gibson。他有很棒的时事通讯，网址是Askgibbs.substack.com。Ian，非常感谢你今天的到来。这次交流太棒了。真的很感激你能和我们分享这些智慧。最后两个问题。如果大家想联系你、了解更多信息，或者想为听众提供帮助，该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: Yeah, I guess Twitter's a great place. So IanMcAll, I-A-N-M-C-A-L-L, is my handle. And then I've started a newsletter. I'm not that frequent to be honest. I have a lot of good intentions and a bunch of ideas. Ianmcallister.substack.com. And that's something to connect and feel free to subscribe and hit me up on Twitter if you have ideas for posts or questions. And if I can answer in a tweet, I will. If not, I might put it on the queue of things to write about. And yeah, thanks for having me on Lenny. We were talking earlier about writing or doing other things and the value of that is just making connections with people. And so that was what I was one, just to reconnect with you is awesome. And to whatever extent I get a chance to make new connections in the world, that's a good thing.
turns.zh: 是啊，Twitter是个很好的平台。我的账号是IanMcAll，I-A-N-M-C-A-L-L。另外，我刚开了一个时事通讯。说实话，我更新得不算勤。想法很多，灵感也不断。网址是ianmcallister.substack.com。大家可以关注我的账号，有任何投稿或问题，都可以在Twitter上联系我。如果能在推文里回复，我会尽力解答。若不行，我会把问题加入待写清单。总之，感谢Lenny邀请我参加节目。我们之前谈到写作或其他事务的价值，就是在于与人建立联系。所以能与你再次相聚真是太棒了。只要有机会能在世界上建立新的联系，那就是件好事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And we originally connected over that piece that you wrote, so it all circles back 10 years later maybe. Thanks, Ian.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们最初就是因为你写的那篇文章而结缘的，或许十年后一切又回到了原点吧。谢谢你，伊恩。

turns.speaker: Ian McAllister
turns.en: All right. Thanks Lenny.
turns.zh: 好的，谢谢你，莱尼。

turns.en: Thank you so much for listening.
